title_ru: Города для людей, а не для машин
description_ru: Мнение о том, что города должны отдавать больше места пешеходам и велосипедистам: примеры Копенгагена и Боготы, аргументы и решения.
text:
Imagine walking down your street in the evening. There are cars on both sides of the road, and more cars are slowly moving past you, waiting for the traffic lights to change. The air smells of exhaust fumes, and a child on a bicycle looks nervous, because the cars are so close. Now imagine the same street without most of those cars. There are trees, tables outside a café, and children playing on the pavement. I believe that the second picture is not a dream. In my opinion, our cities should be designed for people, not for cars.

Cars have changed our towns more than almost any other invention. In the last hundred years we have built wider roads, bigger car parks and fast ring roads, and we have often destroyed parks and old buildings to do it. The result is that many cities are noisy, polluted and dangerous. According to the World Health Organization, millions of people die every year because of dirty air, and road accidents kill more than a million. Some of these deaths are the price we have paid for convenience, but I do not think that the price is fair.

The usual reply is that cars are necessary. People have to go to work, take their children to school and buy food, and public transport is often slow or expensive. I understand this argument, and I would never say that everybody should give up their car tomorrow. For people who live far away from the centre, or who have disabilities, a car can be essential. However, if we look at the numbers, we find that a large proportion of urban journeys are shorter than five kilometres. For these trips, walking, cycling or taking a tram would be just as fast and much cheaper.

Several cities have already shown that change is possible. In Copenhagen, about half of all people cycle to work or school, because the city has built safe, separate cycle lanes. In Paris, the mayor has turned parts of the river bank into walking areas and has reduced parking in the centre. Bogota in Colombia closes hundreds of kilometres of roads to cars every Sunday so that families can walk, run and cycle. In each of these places, people were worried at first. Shop owners feared that they would lose customers. Yet studies have shown that pedestrians and cyclists often spend more in local shops, because they pass by more slowly and visit more often.

Of course, change does not happen without problems. If a city simply bans cars without offering something better, it will only make people angry. First, there must be a reliable alternative, such as frequent buses, trams and trains that run late at night. Second, the cost of using a car in the centre could be raised, as it has been in London, where drivers pay a daily charge. The money collected can be spent on improving public transport. Third, we should make cycling and walking safer by building wide pavements, good lighting and secure bicycle parking.

I also think that we should consider the effect on our health and happiness. People who walk or cycle every day are fitter and often feel less stressed. Children who can play outside without fear learn to be independent, and older people are less lonely when they can easily meet neighbours in a pleasant square. If a street is quiet, people talk to one another. When I lived near a busy road, I did not know a single person in my building. Since I moved to a pedestrian area, I have made five friends.

A quieter city would also sound better. Anyone who has tried to talk on a busy pavement or sleep with the window open knows how tiring constant traffic noise can be. Naturally, a city with fewer cars cannot work if people are not willing to change their habits. We have become used to jumping in the car for every little journey, even when a walk would take ten minutes. But habits can change. Twenty years ago many people smoked in restaurants, and today that seems unthinkable. I suspect that in another twenty years we will look at crowded, car-filled streets with the same surprise.

To sum up, I am not against cars, and I do not claim that they have no uses. What I would like is for them to become guests in our cities, rather than owners. If we give more space to people, with parks, bicycles, trams and wide pavements, our cities will be cleaner, safer and friendlier. It will take time and courage, but I am convinced that it will be worth it.

questions.question: What do many urban journeys have in common?
questions.answer: They are shorter than five kilometres.

questions.question: What have Copenhagen and Bogota done?
questions.answer: Copenhagen built safe cycle lanes, and Bogota closes roads to cars on Sundays.

questions.question: What three steps does the author suggest?
questions.answer: Reliable public transport, higher costs for cars in the centre, and safer walking and cycling.

questions.question: How did the author's life change after moving to a pedestrian area?
